1. Trouble in the Corinthian church
 - In Ephesus there was great revival and growth, but trouble broke out in the Corinthian church. So it seems Paul wrote about four letters to sort it out. Paul visited three times, Timothy visited, Titus visited, and they worked hard to settle the problems, but the Corinthian church was a really difficult church.
바울이 쓴 고린도 전서를 디모데가 직접 가지고 갑니다. 그래서 고린도전서: Timothy personally carries 1 Corinthians, which Paul wrote. So 1 Corinthians was written along the lines of "handle the Corinthian church's various problems like this, and like this." If you look from chapter 1, after the greeting up to verse 9, he goes straight into pointing out the Corinthian church's problems one by one.

1) Factional conflict
 - When Paul left after about a year and a half of ministry, he thought, ‘After this much, they'll be able to manage well on their own,’ and he took all his staff, even Priscilla and Aquila, with him to Ephesus. So the Corinthian church became really empty.
11절부터 보시면 글로에 편으로 얘기를 들어보니 너희 가운데 분쟁이 있다: If you look from verse 11, he says he heard from those of the house of Chloe that there are contentions among you, right? 12. Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ...
바울과 스텝들이 떠난 고린도에 아볼로가 와서 사역을 하니까 굉장히 인기를:
After Paul and his staff left Corinth, Apollos came and ministered there, and he became very popular. Apollos was learned, eloquent, and good-looking, so people who liked Apollos came along.
 - On the other hand, the people who had received grace through Paul said, ‘Apollos is good, sure, but there's not much substance,’ and so a Paul faction formed too.
 - With the Paul faction and the Apollos faction fighting each other, some others said Paul isn't even an apostle and Apollos is just an unknown evangelist, and a Cephas faction formed. Then others said, ‘No, forget Paul and all the rest, we don't need any of them. Christ is the best,’ and a Christ faction formed.

Coming from a somewhat polytheistic background, just as philosophy has its schools, they were very proud of saying ‘I learned under so-and-so.’ The problem is that this culture came right into the church as it was. Paul tells them to knock it off, fast.

3) Lawsuits between believers, chapter 6
 - Believers were suing and filing charges against each other over their interests. We need to understand a bit of Greek culture here: for these people, going to court was an everyday thing. They took pride, as civilized citizens, in going before a judge and settling even trivial matters through a trial. Every neighborhood had a small court called the bema, and they'd sue over even petty things.

I mean, people who are going to judge angels, over a few measly coins, take each other to a worldly court and sit hunched like criminals before a judge who doesn't even believe, to be judged by him? Does that even make sense? Just take the loss instead. What do you think you're doing?

Here's why: they were heavily influenced by the hedonism of the Epicurean school, and they believed the spirit is not affected by the flesh. So they said basic human desires like sexual desire should be satisfied whenever they come up. Just like eating when you're hungry.

 4) The question of believers' marriage

Look at chapter 7 verse 1: "Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me..." These words come up, right? So Paul and the Corinthian church exchanged letters several times. And the theme of chapter 7 is the question of believers' marriage, right? So we can infer that what the Corinthian church asked Paul by letter was something like: is it right to get married, or right not to?
- Paul once said it's good to stay single like him, and that turned into something like a doctrine, so a "you may marry" faction and a "you may not marry" faction formed. As I said earlier, early in his ministry Paul thought Jesus would come any minute, so he said there was no need to bother getting married. Also, before long Emperor Nero's horrific persecution would begin, and having a wife and children would make things harder, so that's why he said it. But they misunderstood it and treated it like a doctrine that must be kept, and they fought each other over it.
Paul's conclusion is: if at all possible, it's better to stay single, but if you really can't hold back, get married. And those who are already married, take good care of your family. That's it.

 6) The question of Paul's apostleship
 - "Paul goes around calling himself an apostle." Paul didn't take any pay so as not to be a burden on this Corinthian church. So they pick at Paul, saying, ‘He didn't take it because he's not an apostle. If he were an apostle, he'd have taken it with a big show, wouldn't he?’

7) The head covering women wear, chapter 11
 - The tradition Paul had passed on to them was that men should not cover their heads and women should wear a veil on their heads. Women wore it as a sign that they themselves were under the authority of men, you see. At the time, married women wore it on their heads as a sign that they were married. Basically, Hebrew thought regarded a woman's hair as something sexual. So from as young as 13 they covered their hair, and after that no one but their husband could see it. Paul thought of uncovering the hair as almost like going around with your chest uncovered, so how shocking must it have been for him to go to Corinth? So Paul passed this on in Corinth too.
그런데 어떤 여자들이 우린 못쓰겠다 이렇게 나왔는가봐요. 그래서 바울이:
But it seems some women came out saying, we won't wear it. So Paul says it again, firmly: over the woman is the man, over the man is Christ, over Christ is God. The woman came from the man.
- Those who have a different opinion, take note. We, and all the churches of God, have received this ordinance.
